stem: Justify the placement of hydrogen in the group of alkali metals with the help of reaction with halogens.
solution:
Hydrogen on reaction with halogen \((\mathrm{X_2})\) gives compounds with general formula HX. For example :

\(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

Similarly alkali metals (M) on reaction with halogens \((\mathrm{X_2})\) give compounds with general formula MX.

For examples : \(2\mathrm{Na} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

Thus, \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and alkali metal are monovalent elements more electropositive than halogens. This similarity justifies the place of hydrogen in the group 1.
_note: p-02, printed p.112, right column blue box.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: Sodium forms ionic compounds having formulae \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), \(\mathrm{NaH}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}\). Explain.
solution:
Let us rewrite the formulae of the compounds of sodium showing charges on the concerned cation and basic anion.

\(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}\),  \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}H^{\ominus}}\),  \(2\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\ \mathrm{CO_3^{2\ominus}}\)

It is seen that in all these compounds Na carries one positive charge. The \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) is formed from Na atom by losing one electron.

\(\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{e^{\ominus}}\)

This happens because the electronic configuration of Na is \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^1\). There is only one electron in the valence shell of Na. It can easily be lost as the ionization enthalpy is low. And \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) ion so formed is stable as it has stable electronic configuration of the inert gas Ne.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: Explain the observed values 496 kJ/mol and 737 kJ/mol of the first ionization enthalpies of Na and Mg, respectively.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the printed solution reads "The resulting Na is isoelectronic with Ne". Neutral sodium has eleven electrons and is not isoelectronic with neon; what is meant is the ion \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\), which the same solution has just formed and which does have neon's ten-electron configuration. The charge has been dropped in that one sentence — the two ionisation equations printed directly above it carry it correctly. The book also prints "iouization" for "ionization" and "Thats" for "That's"; those are pure spelling and have been normalised here. The reasoning and the conclusion are unaffected.]

The electronic configuration of Na is \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^1\) and that of Mg is \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2\). During the first ionization only one electron is removed from a neutral atom.

\(\mathrm{Na} \xrightarrow{1^{\text{st}}\ \text{ionisation}} \mathrm{Na^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{e^{\ominus}}\)

\(\mathrm{Mg} \xrightarrow{1^{\text{st}}\ \text{ionisation}} \mathrm{Mg^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{e^{\ominus}}\)

The resulting Na is isoelectronic with Ne, and therefore, is stable. That's why Na has low value of 1st ionization enthalpy. However, to form the unipositive \(\mathrm{Mg^{\oplus}}\) ion energy is required to unpair these electrons in the valency shell and also remove one electron to form the ion having electronic configuration \([\mathrm{Ne}]\ 3s^1\). It is not as stable as Na since it does not correspond to any inert gas. Therefore the first ionization enthalpy of Mg is higher than that of Na.
_note: p-05, printed p.115, left column lower box. Book prints 'iouization' for 'ionization' and 'Thats' for "That's" — pure spelling, normalised. The bare 'Na' in 'The resulting Na is isoelectronic with Ne' is as printed (verified at 4x against the Na⊕ on the same page) — it means Na⊕; bracketed in errata.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: What is the oxidation state of Na in \(\mathrm{Na_2O_2}\)?
solution: The peroxide species is represented as \(\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}\). Any compound is electrically neutral. Therefore oxidation state of each Na is \((+2/2 = +1)\) in \(\mathrm{Na_2O_2}\).
_note: p-05, printed p.115, right column top box.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: The atomic radii of Na, K and Mg are 186, 227 and 160 pm, respectively. Explain the differences.
solution: Na and K both belong to the group 1. K has larger valence shell than Na. Therefore the atomic radius of K is larger than that of Na. Na and Mg belong to the same period. Therefore both have the same valence shell. But the nuclear charge of Mg is larger than that of Na. Therefore, the valence electrons of Mg are held more tightly and its atomic radius is smaller than that of Na.
_note: p-05, printed p.115, right column second box.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) is an ionic compound but \(\mathrm{LiCl}\) has some covalent character, explain.
solution: \(\mathrm{Li^{\oplus}}\) ion has very small size, therefore the charge density on \(\mathrm{Li^{\oplus}}\) is high. Therefore it has high tendency to distort the electron cloud around the negatively charged large chloride ion. This results in partial covalent character of the LiCl bond. \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) ion cannot distort the electron cloud of \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) due to the bigger size of \(\mathrm{Na^{\oplus}}\) compared to \(\mathrm{Li^{\oplus}}\).
_note: p-06, printed p.116, right column. The 'Problem 8.6' label is split across three text-layer lines, which is why a naive `Problem 8.\d` scan misses its number.

subtopic: Alkali Metals and Alkaline Earth Metals
stem: Magnesium strip slowly tarnishes on keeping in air but metallic calcium is readily attacked by air. Explain.
solution:
[Textbook answer-key error: the printed solution states that "Mg and Ca belong to group 2, but periods 2 and 3, respectively". Both period numbers are wrong: magnesium (atomic number 12, condensed configuration \([\mathrm{Ne}]3s^2\) in this chapter's own Table 8.3) is in period 3, and calcium (atomic number 20, \([\mathrm{Ar}]4s^2\)) is in period 4. The chapter's Table 8.3 contradicts the printed sentence directly. The explanation that follows does not depend on the numbers — it turns only on calcium lying BELOW magnesium in the group, which remains true — so the answer stands and the working is preserved as printed.]

Mg and Ca belong to group 2, but periods 2 and 3, respectively. During the reaction with air the metallic Mg and Ca lose their valence electrons. The tendency to lose valence electron is the metallic character, which increases down the group. Thus, calcium has higher metallic character, greater tendency to lose valence electron and lower ionization enthalpy than magnesium. Therefore Mg reacts slowly with air, forming a thin film of oxide, resulting into tarnishing, whereas Ca reacts readily at room temperature with oxygen and nitrogen in the air.
_note: p-09, printed p.119, left column. The 'periods 2 and 3' clause is a printed factual error (Mg is period 3, Ca period 4) — verified at 4x; preserved as printed and bracketed in errata.

subtopic: Some Important Compounds of s-Block Elements
stem: Calculate % (by mass) of a \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) solution which is 45.4 volume.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book labels this worked example "Promblem 8.8" — the only one of the chapter's eight worked examples whose label is misspelled, and the reason a scan of the chapter finds seven "Problem" labels against eight "Solution" labels. Separately, the last line divides by "1000 g water" when the quantity required is a percentage by mass of SOLUTION, not of water; what is being assumed is that 1 L of the solution has a mass of about 1000 g. The arithmetic and the answer are unaffected — \(68 \times 45.4 / 22.7 = 136\) exactly, and \(136/1000 = 13.6\%\) — so the working is preserved as printed.]

45.4 volume \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) solution means 1 L of this solution will give 45.4 L \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP.

\(2\,\mathrm{H_2O_2} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{H_2O} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

\((2 \times 34)\ \mathrm{g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) gives \(22.7\ \mathrm{L}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP.

Thus, \(22.7\ \mathrm{L}\) \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP is produced by \(68\ \mathrm{g}\) \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)

\(\therefore\ 45.4\ \mathrm{L}\) \(\mathrm{O_2}\) at STP is produced by \(\dfrac{68 \times 45.4}{22.7} = 136\ \mathrm{g}\) \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\)

\(\therefore\) Strength of this \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) solution \(= 136\ \mathrm{g/L}\)

\(= \dfrac{136\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{H_2O_2}}{1000\ \mathrm{g}\ \text{water}} = 13.6\%\) (by mass)
_note: p-11, printed p.121, right column. ⚠ THE BOOK PRINTS 'Promblem 8.8' (misspelled) — this is why the chapter shows 7 `Problem` labels against 8 `Solution` labels. The final line's denominator is labelled '1000 g water'; bracketed in errata.
